title: Run your first simulation
summary: Open the workbench, press play, and see what the controls do.
body:
breve runs small simulations you can change while they run. Nothing to install: open the **Simulations** page and pick one from the list at the top. Start with **Hello: random walkers** ([open it](../sim/#hello)).

## What you are looking at

Sixty walkers wander around a box. Under the picture:

- **Play / Pause**, **Step** (one tick at a time) and **Reset** (start again from the same seed, so the run repeats exactly).
- A **timeline**: drag it to go back to an earlier moment, and play on from there to branch a new run.
- **Controls**: one slider for every number the simulation lets you change. Move *how much each walker wanders* and watch the walkers react at once.
- A **chart** for each number the simulation measures. Here it is *spread*: how far the walkers are from the middle, on average.

Drag in the picture to turn the camera, scroll to zoom. Click a walker to look at it: you can see (and change) its numbers.

The card in the corner (**About**) says what the simulation is. It folds away.

## Try this

1. Set *wander* to 0. Nothing pushes the walkers, so they drift in a straight line until the soft wall turns them back.
2. Set it to 20 and press **Reset** a few times. The seed is fixed, so every reset gives the same run: change the number, not the luck.
3. Pick **Boids** from the list ([open it](../sim/#boids)). Sixty-odd birds follow three rules, and a flock appears. Move *cohesion* and *separation* and see how the flock changes character.

The rest of the guide shows how these are written, so you can change them and make your own. Next: [change something](#/02-change-something).

title: Change something
summary: Edit the scene and the script in the editor drawer, and see the run change as you type.
body:
Every simulation is two small files: a **scene** (the setup and the knobs, written as JSON) and a **script** (what the things in it do, written in JavaScript). Both are editable in the workbench.

## Open the editor

Click the **Editor** tab on the left edge, press **E**, or click **Editor** in the header. It slides out over the picture; drag its right edge to make it wider, and press **Esc** or click the tab again to put it away. It has tabs for `scene.json`, `script.js` and `experiment.json`.

## Edit the scene

`scene.json` opens as a tree. Find `entities`, open the first one, and change `count` from 60 to 300. The run restarts with 300 walkers. Switch to the text view (**Text view**) if you prefer to type JSON; the two stay in step.

Under `params` is the slider you were just using. Change its `value` (where the slider starts), `min` or `max`, or add another one: any number you put in `params` becomes a slider, and your script reads it as `p.name`.

If you make a mistake, the problems list says what and where in words, and the last good version keeps running.

## Edit the script

Open `script.js`. The heart of it is one function:

```js
act({ self }, p, ctx) {
  const wander = ctx.vec(ctx.random() - 0.5, ctx.random() - 0.5, ctx.random() - 0.5).times(p.wander)
  return { steer: wander.plus(ctx.bounds.soft(self.position, ctx.world.size)) }
}
```

Every tick, every walker gets this call. `self` is the walker, `p` the sliders, `ctx` a toolbox. It returns a **steer**: a push. Try:

- Delete `.plus(ctx.bounds.soft(...))`. With no wall, walkers escape the box.
- Change `ctx.random() - 0.5` in the middle term to `0`. The walkers now wander only in two directions.
- Add `.plus(self.velocity.times(-0.5))` after `wander`. That is friction: they slow down.

The simulation updates a moment after you stop typing. **Restore example** (next to the project name) puts the original back whenever you want.

Next: [how a simulation is written](#/03-how-a-simulation-is-written).

title: How a simulation is written
summary: Four small hooks, a rule that nothing changes behind your back, and a toolbox.
body:
A script exports a **controller**: an object with up to four functions.

| hook | when it runs | what it returns |
|---|---|---|
| `init` | once, as each thing is made | what it starts as: `{ hunger: 0 }` |
| `act` | every tick | what it wants to do: a `steer`, and any new state |
| `think` | every so often, slowly (it may ask a language model) | what it decided, as state |
| `display` | when drawing | how it looks: a color, a size |

## The one rule

**A script never changes anything. It returns what it wants, and the engine does it for everyone at once.** Every walker sees the world as it was at the start of the tick, so the order they are asked in makes no difference. It is also why runs can be repeated exactly, copied mid-run, and replayed.

## Keeping state

Whatever `init` returns becomes the thing's state, readable as `self.hunger`. To change it, return the new value from `act`:

```js
export default {
  init() { return { hunger: 0 } },

  act({ self }, p, ctx) {
    const wander = ctx.vec(ctx.random() - 0.5, ctx.random() - 0.5, ctx.random() - 0.5).times(p.wander)
    return {
      steer: wander.plus(ctx.bounds.soft(self.position, ctx.world.size)),
      state: { hunger: self.hunger + 1 },
    }
  },

  display({ self }, p, ctx) {
    // blue when fresh, red when hungry
    return { color: ctx.colors.gradient(['#4f86f7', '#ff5a4d'], self.hunger / 300) }
  },
}
```

Paste that over `script.js` in the Hello example: the walkers turn from blue to red as the ticks go by.

## Looking at others

Things that move freely can see their neighbors. In **Boids** the rule is a few lines about the group of birds nearby:

```js
const cohesion = neighbors.offset.average()                     // toward the middle of the group
const alignment = neighbors.velocity.minus(self.velocity).average()  // how they move compared to me
```

Groups answer questions like `neighbors.velocity.average()` with no loops.

## The toolbox

- `ctx.random()`: the seeded random number. **Never use `Math.random()`**: a run must come out the same every time.
- `ctx.vec(x, y, z)` makes a vector; vectors have `plus`, `minus`, `times`, `length`, `normalized` and more, and always make a new one.
- `p.name` is the current value of the slider called `name`.
- `ctx.tick` is the tick number. `ctx.bounds` keeps things in a box, `ctx.colors` makes colors.
- `export const metrics = { spread: ({ agents }) => ... }` names a number to chart; list its name under `metrics` in the scene.

The full list is the script reference, `docs/script-api.md` in the repository.

Next: [other kinds of worlds](#/04-other-kinds-of-worlds).

title: Other kinds of worlds
summary: Free agents, grids of cells, networks, and bodies with physics: the same script ideas on each.
body:
The scene says what kind of thing each *entity set* is. The script hooks stay the same.

## Free agents

What you have used so far: things with a position and a velocity that move in space (flocks, ants, herds, markets of wandering traders). `count` says how many.

## Grids of cells

Add a `lattice` to an entity set and every cell is an entity that sees its neighbors. **2D Life** is a grid; **Gray-Scott** grows patterns on one. A cell's `act` returns its new state, for example `{ alive: 1 }`. Edges can wrap around.

## Networks

A `network` is nodes joined by links, and a node sees the nodes it is linked to. **Epidemic** spreads a disease along links; the *same script* also runs it on a grid of cells, because it only asks "who are my neighbors, and how many are infected?".

## Bodies with physics

Give an entity a `body` (boxes, spheres, hinge joints with motors) and it becomes a creature in a physics world with terrain. **Creature** is a jointed body walking on terrain; **Evolved creatures** runs a whole population side by side and breeds the best walkers. The physics engine is chosen in the scene (`"physics": { "engine": "mujoco" }`), and a script can run a *population* of simulations, each with its own camera tile, from a parent script.

## Several at once

A scene can hold several sets at once: ants, food, a nest, and the ground they leave scent on are four sets in **Ants**, each with its own small script.

Where to look next: the **Gallery** shows every example with a picture; each one has an **About** card, and opening it puts all of its code in your editor. Next: [making it fast](#/05-making-it-fast).

title: Making it fast
summary: Per-thing rules for learning, whole-grid rules for big grids, and formulas that run on a graphics card.

title: Share it and keep going
summary: Fork an example into your own project, send a link, and where the reference lives.
body:
## Make it yours

**Fork** copies the example you are looking at into **My projects**, where your edits are saved in your browser and stay yours. Give it a name in the box next to the picker. The original is untouched, and **Restore example** brings back an example's own version whenever you want.

## Share it

**Share** copies a link that carries the whole scene and script. Whoever opens it gets your project in their workbench. Because a script is code, a project that arrives from a link **is not run** until its reader has had a chance to read the script and press **Run the script**.

## Test an idea

**Sweep** runs the same scene many times with different slider values side by side and shows them as tiles, so you can see the effect of a number without moving it back and forth. Click a tile to continue from that run.

## Keep going

- The **Gallery** has an example of each kind of world.
- The **Blog** tells how some of the examples were made, including what went wrong.
- The script reference is `docs/script-api.md` in the repository, and the standard library (vectors, colors, bounds, neural nets, fields) is documented in `docs/stdlib.md`.
- The source is on GitHub. The principle behind the design is on the About page: *all models are wrong, some are useful*. A simulation is a model, and breve is built to make it quick to change what you think is wrong.
